name: Radio Equipment Directive
evidence_rating: thin: compliance indicator partially tracked through targeted (non-representative) inspections; burden and innovation indicators not measured; no independent studies found
summary: The Radio Equipment Directive promised higher product compliance with little extra burden. Market surveillance data show around 60% of inspected products failing in 2022, but because inspectors target risky products this does not show whether compliance has improved since the 28-56% baseline. The promised indicators on red tape and innovation were never measured, and no independent study was found.

indicators.indicator: Administrative and technical compliance ratios (periodic Member State reports)
indicators.target_or_baseline: Baseline (IA): 28-56% compliance with essential requirements in market surveillance campaigns; of 6,168 R&TTE items inspected, 68% met essential requirements
indicators.evidence: ADCO RED statistics: 11,491 inspections in 2022 with about 60% non-compliance, but inspections target problem sectors so not representative. 2018 report found no category with demonstrably low compliance; 2024 report says self-assessment 'has led to low levels of compliance' according to stakeholders.

indicators.indicator: Induced administrative cost and burden; number of interpretation issues
indicators.evidence: No quantified burden estimate in either operation report; interpretation issues handled via guidance and expert group.
Only stakeholder survey views in the 2024 report; no systematic measure.

literature.citation: European Commission (2012), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on radio equipment, SWD(2012) 329 (executive summary SWD(2012) 300)
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on radio equipment
literature.headline: Baseline compliance with essential requirements of only 28-56% in surveillance campaigns; revision expected to raise compliance via traceability and registration with limited extra burden
literature.summary_plain: The Commission found that up to half of radio devices checked broke the rules and expected the revised directive to raise compliance at little extra cost.
literature.verified: full text read (executive summary; IA tables checked)

literature.citation: European Commission (2018), Report on the operation of the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU, COM(2018) 740
literature.title: Report on the operation of the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU
literature.headline: Too early to judge effectiveness; manufacturers used the old directive during transition; no evidence of any category with low compliance
literature.summary_plain: The first review, a year after the transition, said it was too early to judge the directive's effects.

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Second Report on the operation of Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU, COM(2024) 158
literature.title: Second Report on the operation of Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU
literature.method: monitoring report (Article 47; ADCO statistics, stakeholder survey)
literature.headline: 11,491 inspections in 2022 with about 60% non-compliance (targeted, not representative); stakeholders say self-assessment has led to low compliance; common charger (USB-C) amendment adopted 2022
literature.summary_plain: The second review reports that about 60% of radio products inspected in 2022 failed checks, though inspectors target risky products, and stakeholders doubt self-certification works.
